lines: The cold goes first. Then the noise. Then the part of me that was worried about the noise.
What is left over is standing in a corridor that is all filing and no building, under a ceiling too far up to be a ceiling.
Nothing hurts. I would like it on record that I find this deeply suspicious.

hollow_court_first.art_desc: The Hollow Court: a translucent clerk at a lamplit desk before endless filing shelves, one empty chair facing him
lines: A desk. A lamp. A queue of one, and the one is me.
The Clerk does not look up. 'Name?'
answers: 'Everyone here is something.' He turns a page without touching it, and then stops turning it.

'Nine.' He looks at me over the spectacles for the first time. 'You have NINE.' He checks the sheet again, and then a second sheet, and his face does what a clerk's face does when the arithmetic is somebody else's problem.
'...Vane's familiar. Well. That is what it says.' He writes it down exactly as written. 'Nine allotted. One spent.'
'Needle Lane.' Something moves behind the spectacles that is almost interest. 'Yes. We have had a busy evening from Needle Lane.'
Then he reaches the column that matters and stops. 'Nine allotted.' He says it to the paper, not to me. 'I have not filed a nine since I was at a much smaller desk.'
'Vane's familiar. One spent.' He does not say whose the busy evening was. I do not ask. Not here.
The silence goes on long enough to become a position. He allows it, and writes anyway.
Halfway down he stops. 'Nine,' he says, to nobody. He turns the sheet over as though the back might explain it. It does not.
'Vane's familiar. Nine allotted, one spent.' — 'You will find that not answering is also an answer, and that I have a great deal of filing.'

lines: 'The arrangement, since it is your first: you are difficult to kill and not impossible. When you are killed you come here, we take the Toll, and you go back up.'

lines.text: Dying costs a life and a quarter of the shine you have banked at home. Whatever you were carrying stays where you dropped it. Nothing else is lost — not your kit, not your case, not what you have already worked out.

lines: 'The first visit is complimentary. Do consider it a courtesy rather than a habit.'
The stamp comes down. It is, I notice, a paw print. Neither of us remarks on this.

hollow_court_first.art_desc: A narrow stone stair climbing out of the Hollow Court's filing dark towards a small warm doorway far above, one black cat starting up it
lines: The stairs up are longer
than the fall down.
They always are.
The desk again. The lamp again. He does not look up.
'Back so soon. The form remembers you, which saves us both time.'
The Toll is taken. Professionally. Almost gently.
Third. He has the stamp out before I reach the chair, which I choose to find efficient rather than insulting.
'You are making a habit of an arrangement,' he says. 'Habits are how arrangements become entitlements. I mention it only professionally.'
I sit anyway. He lets me.
'Four,' says the Clerk, and for once does not write it down immediately.
'May I ask what you are doing up there?' — I am looking for someone. — 'Ah. Yes. That is the usual answer, and the usual number of lives it takes.'
The stamp comes down softer than it needs to.
He has started keeping my file on the desk rather than in the drawer. Out is worse than filed; he told me so himself, once.
'Halfway,' he says. Not unkindly. That is the trouble with him.
'I am obliged to remind you that the allotment is not a budget. It is a quantity of you.'
There is a chair at the desk that was not there before. It is exactly cat-sized. Neither of us mentions it.
'The Toll,' he says, and takes it, and then sits with his hands folded for a moment longer than the work requires.
'Go carefully. That is not in the form. I am saying it anyway.'
He counts what is left twice. He is not a man who counts twice.
'Two,' he says. 'You will want to know what happens at nought. It is not dramatic. The file closes and the desk is empty and there is a great deal of filing that afternoon.'
'I would rather not do the filing.'
The lamp is turned up. He has turned the lamp up, for me, which is the most alarming thing that has happened tonight.
'One,' says the Clerk. 'I will not lecture you. You know precisely what you are spending and precisely what you are spending it on.'
'Whatever it is up there — do finish it.'

mantel_coach.text: Her parlor. Cold, and still hers. This is where a night begins and, with luck, ends.
What the city wants doing gets pinned to the chimney breast. One thing tonight.
Tap a note to take the work. Whatever you carry back is yours; whatever you are carrying when you fall is not.
Gleam. Buttons, mostly, and the occasional tooth. It buys cards, and it is what the Court takes when you die.
Lives, the spool, and deeds recorded. Watch the spool: it does not refill while you are out.
The Casebook: everything I know, and how I came to know it. There will be more along this wall when I have reason.

unpicked_won: It comes apart. Thread by thread. That was not supposed to happen.
Somewhere below the city, a clerk files something under 'irregular'.
